sections.h2: Which county offices bill property tax for the city of Champaign?
sections.html:
The city of Champaign does not send its own property tax bill. The Champaign County Treasurer, who also acts as Collector, bills every parcel in the city along with the school districts and other taxing districts that share it. Valuation sits with the Champaign County Supervisor of Assessments, and the city is coterminous with Champaign City township, so one township assessor covers the whole municipality.

That arrangement keeps the paperwork simple for a seller. One PIN identifies the parcel, and the same two county offices answer questions whether the house is near Campustown, downtown or on the northwest side near Parkland College.

sections.h2: What is the city of Champaign like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Champaign is a council-manager city of about 23 square miles on high, flat ground in central Illinois, founded in 1855 as West Urbana when the Illinois Central Railroad ran its tracks two miles west of Urbana's downtown. It took the Champaign name when it received a city charter in 1860. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign sits on the east side and Parkland College on the northwest, which gives the market a large student population during the school year.

The economy leans on the university, Research Park, health care and food manufacturing. Kraft's plant is described as one of the largest pasta factories in North America, and technology firms keep offices in the park south of State Farm Center. Champaign Unit 4 School District serves the city, with Champaign Central and Centennial high schools. I-57, I-72 and I-74 meet here, and Willard Airport and the Illinois Terminal rail and bus hub sit within the area.

Weather affects older houses in practical ways. Temperatures top 90 degrees Fahrenheit on about 24 days a year and drop below 0 on about six nights, and the winters are moderately snowy. Roofs and heating systems are the usual items to look at before listing a house built in the 1980s or earlier.

sections.h2: How does Champaign compare with the county in Census numbers?
sections.html:
Renters are the majority in the city, which is the main difference from the rest of Champaign County. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates put the owner-occupied rate at 43.8% in the city and 54.0% across the county.

The city's median home value sits close to the countywide figure, while its rents run higher. A landlord selling a rental near campus will often deal with tenants and a lease cycle, and the tax bill follows the parcel regardless of who lives in it.

sections.h2: When is Champaign property tax due?
sections.html:
Bills are mailed by early May and fall due in two installments. The Treasurer's FAQ gives June 3 and September 3 for the 2025 tax year, and a payment postmarked on the due date is on time. Each coupon carries its own dates, so use the bill in front of you for any later year.

Interest of 1.5% a month applies to late payments, and the Treasurer accepts personal checks through September 30. A returned payment is void and costs $30 plus statutory interest. Cards and eCheck work online or by phone at 217-834-8713, and a fee goes to the processing vendor. In person, the Treasurer's counter is at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana.

sections.h2: How can a Champaign owner challenge an assessment?
sections.html:
The Board of Review takes complaints from July 1 through September 10. Its hours are 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Thursday, or by appointment. Township assessors value a home as of January 1 at one-third of market value, and owners receive change notices from the Supervisor of Assessments before the complaint window opens.

Gather evidence that fits the property. For a house, that means your purchase price if you bought recently, a recent appraisal, and sales of similar homes in the same neighborhood. After September 10 the board reviews the complaints and issues written decisions.

sections.h2: Which parts of Champaign shape the housing market?
sections.html:
Several districts pull demand in different directions, and a buyer's questions change with the street. The ones that stand out in the city's history and layout are these:

  • Downtown Champaign: the historic core around the Virginia Theatre and the City Building, with newer mixed-use buildings and a parking deck added during a revitalization effort.
  • Campustown: the Green Street district beside the university, where high-rise student apartments have opened since 2008.
  • North Prospect: a shopping corridor on the city's northern edge that grew out into former farmland.
  • Northwest and west sides: home to Parkland College and the private St. Thomas More High School.

The city has 60 parks and 11 trails, and the Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District runs buses across Champaign, Urbana and Savoy. Those details help a listing for a family house, while investors selling near campus tend to talk about the rental cycle instead.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can a Champaign homeowner claim?
sections.html:
The Assessment Office lists several homestead reductions, each applied to equalized assessed value before the rate is multiplied:

  • General homestead, $6,000, for a primary residence on January 1.
  • Senior citizens, $5,000, for owners 65 or older by December 31 of the assessment year.
  • Senior assessment freeze, with a maximum household income of $75,000, renewed each year.
  • Persons with disabilities, $2,000.
  • Disabled veterans, scaled by disability rating.
  • Returning veterans, $5,000 for two years.

For forms, call the Assessment Office at 217-384-3760. The office cannot accept faxed or emailed applications. Owners who moved in recently should ask whether an earlier owner's exemption carried over before assuming it did.

sections.h2: What happens if Champaign property tax is not paid?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax is sold to a buyer at the county's annual sale, which the Treasurer's FAQ places on October 30 for amounts still open after 4:30 p.m. on October 29. The house is not sold. After the sale the owner owes the amount sold plus interest and redeems through the County Clerk at 217-384-3722.

The Clerk sends a Take Notice within four months of the sale. State law, in 35 ILCS 200/21-350, sets a redemption period that is generally 3 years from the date of sale, subject to listed exceptions. If the owner does not redeem in time, the buyer may petition the circuit court for a deed.

sections.h2: How do you sell a Champaign house when tax is still due?
sections.html:
Start with the PIN. Ask the Treasurer which installments are paid, and read the closing documents or ask the title company or attorney whether tax is owed for the year. The Treasurer notes that, depending on the closing and recording dates, a bill may be addressed to the previous owner, who must forward it to the new owner.

If installments are open, ask the title company how they will be handled at closing. Knowing the number early gives you room to plan the closing date. For a rental in the city, add the tenants' lease end date to the same checklist.

faqs.q: Does the city of Champaign collect its own property tax?
faqs.a: No. The Champaign County Treasurer bills and collects all property tax for parcels in the city, then distributes it to the taxing districts.

faqs.q: What are the 2025 tax year due dates in Champaign?
faqs.a: June 3 for the first installment and September 3 for the second, according to the Treasurer's FAQ. A payment postmarked on the due date counts as on time.

faqs.q: When can I file an assessment complaint for a Champaign home?
faqs.a: Between July 1 and September 10, with the Champaign County Board of Review, which is open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Thursday.

faqs.q: What is the senior exemption in Champaign?
faqs.a: A $5,000 reduction in equalized assessed value for owners 65 or older by December 31 of the assessment year. A separate freeze applies up to a $75,000 household income.

faqs.q: Is the owner-occupied rate in Champaign higher than the county's?
faqs.a: No. The Census Bureau shows 43.8% owner-occupied in the city and 54.0% across Champaign County for 2020 to 2024.
